nameStory: The 'cinnamon' in cinnamon willowherb comes from the warm, reddish-brown coloration that develops on the stems and leaves as the plant matures, especially in fall. The 'willowherb' part refers to its narrow, willow-like leaves and its membership in a group of plants that were once thought to be related to true willows.
description: Cinnamon willowherb is a slender, upright wildflower that typically grows 1-3 feet tall in wet areas throughout New England. This native plant produces small pinkish-purple flowers along branching stems from summer into fall. As its name suggests, the stems and leaves often develop attractive cinnamon-colored tinges, making it quite distinctive among the willowherb family. It's a quietly beautiful plant that adds delicate color to marshes, stream edges, and other moist spots.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pinkish-purple flowers about 1/4 inch across with four petals that are deeply notched at the tips, giving them a heart-shaped appearance. The flowers cluster along the upper stem branches and have a delicate, papery texture.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that are arranged oppositely on the lower stem and alternately higher up. The leaves feel smooth and thin, with finely toothed edges that you can feel when you run your finger along them.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as an upright, branching plant 1-3 feet tall with a somewhat sprawling habit. The stems are smooth and often develop the characteristic cinnamon or reddish coloration, especially toward the base.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces long, narrow seed capsules that split open to release tiny seeds with fluffy white hairs that catch the wind. The capsules are about 1-2 inches long and dangle from the stem tips.

habitat: Look for cinnamon willowherb in wet soils along stream banks, pond edges, marshes, and ditches throughout New England. It thrives in areas that stay consistently moist and can tolerate some flooding. You'll often find it growing alongside other moisture-loving plants like sedges, jewelweed, and other willowherbs in both sunny and partially shaded locations.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge as small rosettes of narrow leaves in late spring. The characteristic cinnamon coloration isn't yet apparent, making identification more challenging at this stage.
seasonality.summer: Blooming begins in mid to late summer with small pinkish-purple flowers appearing along branching stems. The plant reaches its full height and the stem coloration starts to develop.
seasonality.fall: The distinctive cinnamon-colored stems and leaves are most pronounced in fall. Seed capsules mature and split open, releasing fluffy seeds that drift on autumn breezes.
seasonality.winter: The above-ground parts die back, leaving only the root system to survive the cold. Look for dried seed capsules still clinging to brown stems in protected areas.

funFact: Despite being called a willowherb, this plant is actually in the evening primrose family and is more closely related to fireweed than to willow trees - the name comes from early botanists who thought the narrow leaves looked willow-like, not from any actual relationship!
confusionNotes: Cinnamon willowherb can be tricky to distinguish from other willowherbs, especially fringed willowherb. The key is looking for that telltale cinnamon or purplish coloration on the stems and leaves - if you see reddish-brown tinges, especially in fall, you've likely found cinnamon willowherb rather than its plainer cousins.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'coloratum' literally means 'colored,' referring to the distinctive cinnamon and purplish hues that develop on this species. This plant is also sometimes called purpleleaf willowherb, highlighting the same colorful characteristic that makes it stand out from other willowherbs.
compareHints: Among New England's willowherbs, cinnamon willowherb is distinguished by its colorful stems and leaves - most other willowherbs stay green throughout the season. Great willowherb is much larger with showier flowers, while fringed willowherb lacks the cinnamon coloration. The reddish-brown tints that develop on stems and foliage are your best clue that you've found cinnamon willowherb rather than one of its more plainly colored relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's willowherbs, great willowherb lives up to its name by being the tallest and most robust.
Among New England's willowherbs, fringed willowherb is distinguished by those characteristic tiny hairs along its leaf edges - no other local willowherb has this feature.
Unlike its lowland cousins like great willowherb or cinnamon willowherb, Hornemann's willowherb is much smaller in all respects - shorter stems, tinier flowers, and narrower leaves.
Among New England's willowherbs, linear-leaf willowherb has the narrowest leaves and prefers the wettest habitats.
Among New England's willowherbs, downy willowherb is distinguished by its thoroughly fuzzy texture - much more so than cinnamon willowherb or fringed willowherb.

Among New England willowherbs, hoary willowherb stands out for its overall grayish, densely fuzzy appearance - most other willowherbs like cinnamon willowherb or fringed willowherb are greener with less conspicuous hairs.
Marsh willowherb is much smaller and more delicate than Great Willowherb, which can tower over 6 feet tall with showy magenta flowers.
